headline: CANNRA: DEA's 29 November deadline splits state medical markets
dek: The Cannabis Regulators Association says DEA guidance forcing timely applicants to trade only with each other leaves some states without full supply chains.
key_points: The Cannabis Regulators Association, which groups state cannabis agencies, said on 16 November that DEA guidance has split most state medical markets into a federal track and a state-only track.
DEA's letter tells timely applicants they may deal only with other applicants or registrants, and gives them until 29 November to set up compliant supply chains.
Regulators cite one state where all testing labs applied to the DEA, leaving none for state-only operators, and another where few growers applied, leaving stores without legal supply.
CANNRA says regulators cannot get a named list of applicants from the DEA and have had no substantive engagement from the agency.
body: The officials who license and police state medical cannabis markets have gone public with a warning about the DEA's rollout of Schedule III. In an op-ed published by Marijuana Moment on 16 November, Gillian Schauer, executive director of the Cannabis Regulators Association (CANNRA), wrote that three DEA actions taken in late October have created deep uncertainty for regulators, patients and businesses, and arrived with little or no advance notice to the states.

The sharpest concern is a deadline 13 days away. A DEA letter to timely applicants gives them until 29 November to build supply chains that run only through other timely applicants or DEA registrants. CANNRA says that rule has, almost overnight, split most state medical markets in two, and that in some states neither half has enough growers, makers, labs and stores to function on its own.
## Who CANNRA is, and why this matters

CANNRA is a nonpartisan, nonprofit association of the government agencies that regulate cannabis, marijuana or hemp in more than 45 states, the District of Columbia and three US territories. It does not lobby for the industry. When the regulators themselves say a federal policy makes their markets unworkable, it is a different kind of warning from a trade group complaint.

The op-ed lists the three October actions: guidance to applicants, orders to show cause that challenge whether some applicants can be registered at all, and the first Schedule III medical registrations. MetaFlora covered the first registrations on 6 November and the orders to show cause on 12 November.
## The 29 November rule

The DEA letter, quoted in the op-ed, says timely applicants may not lawfully do Schedule III medical marijuana business with any entity that did not apply for registration between 28 April and 26 June 2026, or has not applied at all, until those entities are registered. Dealing with them could be grounds to deny an application or registration. The DEA's guidance for timely applicants is posted on its Diversion Control website, linked below.

Because almost every state treats moving cannabis across state lines as diversion, a business cannot fill gaps by buying from a neighbouring state. So each state now has two closed loops: a federal one made of DEA registrants and timely applicants, and a state-only one made of licensees who never applied. CANNRA argues many states will not have a complete supply chain in either.
> Schedule III was supposed to pull medical cannabis into the federal system. In practice it is pulling state markets apart first.
## Three states, three gaps

The op-ed gives three examples without naming the states. In one, nearly three-quarters of licensed dispensaries are timely applicants, leaving only a handful of stores in the state-only market. In another, most dispensaries applied but only a few cultivators did, so the federal track would need product from out of state, which that state forbids. In a third, every third-party testing lab applied for DEA registration, leaving no lab at all to test products for state-only businesses.

Each case points to a different failure. Thin state-only retail strands non-applicant growers. Thin federal cultivation strands registered stores. And a state-only market with no labs cannot legally put tested product on a shelf. CANNRA warns that some businesses will survive in neither market, that monopolies could form, that diversion will be harder to detect and that state revenue will fall.
## Regulators flying blind

The DEA has published a list of timely applicants, but only as de-identified registration numbers. CANNRA says regulators have largely been unable to get a list of which businesses in their own state have applied or been registered, and have had to ask licensees for their DEA numbers one by one. MetaFlora's own count of that file on 12 November found 938 pending applications, 613 of them dispensaries, in the six states and Washington, D.C. that were then facing orders to show cause.

Those orders now reach at least seven states or jurisdictions, CANNRA says. The DEA has cited four kinds of state policy: dual licences that let one business serve both medical and adult-use customers, patient self-certification, dispensing without a certification or prescription, and synthetic cannabinoids in the medical supply chain. The orders state that no applicant under such a regime can be registered, but they are arriving unevenly, by mail, in person or by courier, and some states with similar dual-licence rules have received only the timely-applicant letter. Regulators, the op-ed says, are left to guess which states are next.
## What it means for patients

CANNRA flags three patient effects. Self-certification programmes, which often serve hospice patients and veterans whose VA doctors cannot write recommendations, are a main DEA target. The memorandums of agreement that applicants must sign bar dispensing to out-of-state patients, which ends medical reciprocity in the federal track. And a rural patient whose only nearby store applied to the DEA could lose a product if its maker did not. Consumers are noticing: a NuggMD poll we reported this morning found 52% of buyers care whether their dispensary is DEA-registered.
CANNRA says it has raised these issues with the DEA without substantive engagement.
## What to watch

The key date is 29 November, when timely applicants are expected to have compliant supply chains. Watch for state regulators issuing their own guidance on how licensees should handle split supply chains, for more orders to show cause in states with dual licensing or self-certification, and for any DEA move to share named applicant lists with states. The DEA's separate administrative hearing on rescheduling marijuana more broadly, where the agency filed its final brief this month, is a different track and does not by itself change these medical registration rules.
